plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 16: Chemistry of Benzene: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a reaction energy diagram set inside a pale blue rectangular panel, following benzene and bromine along two competing pathways. A tall arrow at the far left, shaded from pale yellow at the bottom to orange at the top, is labeled "Energy"; the horizontal axis beneath the panel reads "Reaction progress" and ends in a magenta arrow. Reactants sit on a dashed level at the left, drawn as a benzene hexagon, a plus sign, and "Br2" in magenta. A black curve climbs from that level to a high first maximum capped by a short dashed line, with a vertical double-headed arrow between maximum and reactant level labeled delta-G double-dagger. The curve drops into a trough, where a cationic intermediate is drawn as a partly unsaturated six-membered ring bearing an H and a magenta Br on the same carbon with a plus sign above it, then rises to a lower second maximum and falls to a dashed product level below the reactants, where bromobenzene plus "HBr" sit above the word "Substitution"; a small double-headed arrow labeled delta-G degrees spans the reactant-to-product gap. From the same trough a magenta curve branches upward over its own maximum and ends above the reactant level at a bracketed dibrominated ring labeled "Addition" and "(does not occur)". Placing both endpoints on one vertical energy scale is what carries the argument: the substitution branch finishes downhill while the addition branch finishes uphill.

Activation free energy ΔG‡ measures the climb from reactants to a transition state, whereas overall free energy ΔG° measures the net energy change from reactants to products

demo_steps.title: Start with benzene and bromine
demo_steps.narration: The reactants begin on the left dashed energy level: benzene plus Br2. The vertical placement sets the reference energy for comparing both possible outcomes.

demo_steps.title: Climb the first barrier
demo_steps.narration: The black curve rises to a high first transition state. The ΔG‡ arrow marks the activation free energy required to reach this unstable arrangement.

demo_steps.title: Form the cationic intermediate
demo_steps.narration: After the first barrier, the reaction reaches a carbocation intermediate. The ring has temporarily lost aromatic stabilization, so this intermediate remains relatively high in energy.

demo_steps.title: Cross the second barrier
demo_steps.narration: The substitution pathway climbs a smaller second barrier as the intermediate moves toward restoring aromaticity. This second peak is lower than the first transition state.

demo_steps.title: Substitution restores aromaticity
demo_steps.narration: The black pathway falls to bromobenzene plus HBr, below the reactant energy level. The negative overall ΔG° shows why substitution is the observed pathway.

demo_steps.title: Compare the addition branch
demo_steps.narration: Switching to the magenta branch shows that addition would end at a higher-energy, nonaromatic product. Because that endpoint is uphill, the addition product is labeled as not occurring.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Both pathways share the same high-energy intermediate, but substitution wins because it restores aromaticity and ends lower in energy, while addition destroys aromaticity and ends uphill.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the original as a pale blue reaction-coordinate panel with energy increasing upward and reaction progress left to right. Use a thick black curve for substitution and a thick magenta curve branching from the intermediate trough for addition. Keep the reactant level dashed on the left, the substitution product level dashed lower on the right, and the addition endpoint visibly higher than the reactants. Color all bromine labels magenta. The stage control should move a bright marker along the chosen curve and glow the corresponding molecular drawing. The pathway toggle should keep both pathways faintly visible but make the selected branch and endpoint bold. Clicking ΔG‡ or ΔG° should emphasize the chosen double-headed arrow and its start/end energy levels so the two energy quantities are visually distinct.

authoredContext:
Why does the reaction of Br2 with benzene take a different course than its reaction with an alkene? The answer is straightforward. If addition occurred, the 150 kJ/mol stabilization energy of the aromatic ring would be lost and the overall reaction would be endergonic. When substitution occurs, though, the stability of the aromatic ring is retained and the reaction is exergonic. An energy diagram for the overall process is shown in the figure.

An energy diagram for the electrophilic bromination of benzene. Because the stability of the aromatic ring is retained, the overall process is exergonic.

Energy diagram shows curve exhibiting two peaks, with the first peak higher than second. A second curve originates from the trough of the first curve and ends higher in energy than the first curve.
